true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently overrides the 4-argument version

`self.downsize` is now defined twice: at line 145 as `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` and again at line 149 as `(from, to, dimensions, opts)`. Ruby keeps only the later definition, so the first is dead code and any caller using the `max_width, max_height` form (the original API) now gets a wrong argument mapping: `max_height` lands in `opts` and the call fails or behaves incorrectly. Only the 3-argument form used by uploads_controller works. Remove one definition and keep a single signature.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side size limit now hardcoded to 10MB, removing the per-type site setting

The `max_' + type + '_size_kb` site setting lookup was replaced with a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. Admins who configured `max_image_size_kb` or `max_attachment_size_kb` will see their settings ignored in the browser, which is a regression. The server still enforces its own limits, so the client now disagrees with the configured policy.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated downsize passes a percentage to gifsicle --resize-fit

The controller calls `downsize(..., "80%", allow_animation: ...)`. For GIFs, `optimize` routes to `downsize_instructions_animated`, which calls `resize_instructions_animated` and emits `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. gifsicle's `--resize-fit` expects a WxH geometry, not a percentage, so the resize fails. `convert_with` returns false, the controller ignores that, and animated GIFs over the limit are never reduced. Animated GIFs need a separate code path or an explicit scale that gifsicle accepts.

true_positives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Downsize loop ignores failure and retries the same conversion up to 5 times

`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns false when conversion fails (`convert_with` swallows errors), but the loop doesn't check the return value. A failed conversion leaves the file unchanged, so the loop runs all five attempts on identical input, wasting time, and then proceeds to `Upload.create_for` with an oversized file. The loop should stop on failure, and the oversized case should be reported to the user rather than silently accepted. Also, `tempfile.size` may be stale if the tool replaces the file rather than rewriting it in place, so the loop condition needs verification.

false_positives.candidate:
API URL download limit changed from the site setting to a hardcoded 10MB

The remote URL download cap was switched from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a fixed `10.megabytes`. This changes the API contract: admins who lowered the image size setting no longer constrain downloads, and the 10MB cap is not configurable.

Client rejects files over 10MB before the server can downsize them

The feature is meant to accept large images and shrink them server-side, but this client check rejects any file larger than 10MB before upload. Users uploading large images will still see the error, so the feature is ineffective from the UI. The check needs to allow images above the limit (or skip it for images) to match the server behavior.

HTTP 413 message now hardcodes 10MB instead of the configured image limit

The 413 branch previously showed `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. It now always displays 10 MB, so the error text can disagree with the actual configured limit that the server enforces.

No tests for the new large-image downsize path

The change adds automatic downsizing in the upload controller, changes the `OptimizedImage` method signatures, and changes client validation, but the PR includes no specs. Nothing covers the loop, its failure handling, animated GIFs, or the duplicate `downsize` definition.

PR description is not meaningful

The description is only 'Test 1'. It does not explain the behavior change, the removal of the site-setting-based limits, or the 10MB hardcoding, so reviewers cannot assess the intent.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validator has a side effect: every validation increments blocked match stats

EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value), which writes match_count and last_match_at on each call. Validations run on every valid? / save, including repeated calls within one request, failed saves for unrelated reasons, and the validation in change_email paths. The statistics therefore count validation attempts rather than actual blocked registrations, and every validation issues a write. Validation should be read-only; the counter update belongs in the actual registration path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, so case variants bypass the block

should_block? does an exact `where(email: email)` match, and the uniqueness validation on BlockedEmail is also case-sensitive. User emails are normalized with Email.downcase elsewhere in the codebase (find_by_username_or_email, change_email), but blocked entries are stored and matched as typed. An entry for 'bad@spamclub.com' will not match 'Bad@SpamClub.com', so a blocked address can register by changing its case. Normalize both the stored value and the lookup (e.g. downcase), or use a case-insensitive comparison.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count loses increments

should_block? loads the record, does `match_count += 1` in Ruby, and calls save. Concurrent signups with the same blocked email race and lose updates. The save also runs validations, so if validation fails the counter silently is not persisted. Use an atomic SQL update such as BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?') or update_counters, which skips validations.

Whitelist/blacklist domain logic moved here without any spec coverage

The domain whitelist/blacklist checks were moved from User into EmailValidator, and the old email_validator behaviour is now only exercised by this file's two blocked-email examples. Nothing tests that email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist still reject addresses, nor that a blocked email is also rejected when it is on a whitelisted domain. Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding NOT NULL column with default rewrites entire posts table

add_column with default and null: false on a large posts table locks and rewrites every row in PostgreSQL on older versions, blocking writes during deploy on large forums.

Anonymous requests can enqueue unbounded retrieve jobs

For any unknown embed_url, `best` enqueues a :retrieve_topic job for every request. The throttle is applied only inside the job (retrieved_recently? via redis), so a flood of distinct URLs on the embeddable host queues an unbounded number of jobs, each performing an outbound HTTP fetch.

Disqus import no longer applies category option and removes the option entirely

The --category option was deleted and the category handling removed, but the import now calls TopicEmbed.import_remote which fetches each thread's live URL instead of creating topics from the XML data. Imports now depend on network access to the old site and ignore the Disqus message content, a behavior change not reflected in the description or help text.

Kernel#open on a fetched URL in import_remote

`open(url).read` is used on an URL that comes from embed requests (TopicRetriever passes the embed_url from an unauthenticated controller parameter, validated only by host). Kernel#open with a crafted string and no timeout can hang or execute commands on old Rubies, and the fetch has no size or time limit.

No test for security-relevant behavior: HTML injection through URL and raw content

The spec asserts raw_html rendering but never tests that the embed URL is escaped in the footer or that script content is neutralized. The security regressions introduced by raw_html storage are unchecked.

PollFeed item processing and error paths are untested

Only the guard conditions and delegation are tested. poll_feed (parsing items, falling back to i.id, CGI unescaping, import) has no coverage, and the spec requires an unrelated process_post job file.

Port handling drops explicit default ports inconsistently and prefix may be built on nil host

`uri.host` is nil for URLs without a host, and the `prefix << ':port'` line mutates a string that may be frozen in some configurations. Also non-default ports on https (443 check only applies to one scheme) produce wrong absolute URLs for http on 443 or https on 80.

Raw HTML from remote feeds/pages stored and rendered without sanitization

Posts created by import use cook_method raw_html, so `Post#cook` returns the raw content unchanged. Content comes from remote RSS feeds or fetched third-party pages (import_remote uses Readability output, but PollFeed passes `i.content` directly). Script or event-handler markup from an untrusted source is rendered to all viewers of the topic and in the embed iframe, a stored XSS vector.

Success assertions run in an after hook and do not verify the behaviour under test

The `after` block asserts response success and headers, but after blocks in the success context also run for the test that expects TopicRetriever and for the TopicView test where render behaviour differs. Failures are reported confusingly and the tests do not check that the loading template is rendered on the retrieve path.

Throttle key set with setnx then expire is non-atomic

setnx followed by a separate expire can leave the key without a TTL if the process dies between calls, permanently throttling that URL. Use SET with NX and EX in one command.

Unique index on embed_url with no length guard for string column

embed_url is a varchar with no length limit, and a unique btree index on long URLs can exceed PostgreSQL's index row size limit, causing inserts of long embed URLs to fail with an error that is not handled in TopicEmbed.import.

contents mutated in place with <<

`contents << ...` mutates the caller's string. In PollFeed, `content` is built once per item and reused; in TopicRetriever/import_remote the doc.content string is mutated, and the sha1 comparison on re-import now includes the footer added each time, so the footer is appended on every import call to the same string object.

embeddable_host and feed settings exposed without validation

embeddable_host is an unvalidated string used as the sole referer check and also to decide which hosts to fetch from. No default validation or type constraint exists, so an admin mistake (e.g. a bare wildcard or empty string on a site that does not set it) can open the embed endpoint to any host.

force: true on create_table will drop existing top_topics data

Adding force: true means that rerunning or running this migration on an installation where the table exists silently drops and recreates it, deleting all TopTopic rows without any warning.

open() of user-configured URL with Kernel#open allows command injection on old Rubies and no timeout

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses Kernel#open, which on Ruby versions before 3.0 treats strings starting with '|' as shell commands. The URL is an admin setting, but it also has no timeout, so a hung feed server blocks the scheduled job indefinitely. Use URI.open or a Net::HTTP call with timeouts.

raw_html posts skip the cooking pipeline and plugin filters entirely

cook returns raw when cook_method is raw_html, bypassing Plugin::Filter :after_post_cook and all sanitization. Any post set to this method, including ones edited later, is stored unsanitized, and the before_save hook also calls cook so edits reuse raw content. Combined with the import path this is a security regression across the whole post model.

save with skip_validations silently ignores failures

`@post.save(validate: ...)` return value is ignored, so a failed save (for example a validation error when skip_validations is false) leaves the in-memory post changed and save_reply_relationships still runs, and the caller receives true from revise!. Errors go unreported.

Jobs are serialized through Sidekiq, so args keys become strings after serialization in some paths; `args[:user_id]` and `args[:embed_url]` may be nil, causing the InvalidParameters raise or silently skipping the user lookup.

Fallback chain reads SiteSetting on every translation lookup

FallbackLocaleList#[] builds a new array by reading SiteSetting.default_locale and calling to_sym each time it is invoked. I18n consults the fallback list on every missing-key lookup, and ensure_loaded! calls it again on every request via set_locale. This adds avoidable work on a hot path. Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain, so cached results can be stale

The LRU cache key is built from key, config.locale and the backend object_id only. With fallbacks now dependent on SiteSetting.default_locale, a translation resolved through the fallback chain is cached under a key that does not include the default locale. If default_locale changes at runtime, previously cached fallback results keep being served for that process until reload!. The key also concatenates without a separator, so distinct (key, locale) pairs can collide, for example key 'a' with locale 'en' versus key 'ae' with locale ''.

It walks the fallback list and calls I18n.ensure_loaded! for each locale, which takes the LOAD_MUTEX path when a locale is not yet marked loaded. The work is cheap once loaded, but it repeats the SiteSetting read and array construction on every request. Loading could happen once per locale instead of per request.

The new endpoint tests rely on the 60-second cache inside is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects without clearing it, so results depend on test ordering across the allowlist cases. Also setUp overwrites self.user after creating projects and assigns self.authed_user before reassigning, and the count assertions (10 per bucket) are not derived from the stored events, which contain only one event per bucket, so the expected value of 10 is suspicious and likely wrong.

Misleading comments claim caching and late optimization that do not exist

The comments say the cached result ensures consistent behavior and that the separation enables caching and query optimization; no such caching of the upsampling decision across query execution exists, the decision is recomputed per call. These comments will mislead maintainers.

Stray submodule pointer committed to repository root

A file named sentry-repo is added containing a gitlink-style 'Subproject commit' line pointing at the base commit. This is unrelated to error upsampling and will break or confuse checkouts/tooling that does not expect a submodule at that path.

Tests create organization and projects with unused fixtures and do not test cache or is_errors_query path

The main entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects and its caching behavior, plus invalidate_upsampling_cache, are not tested at all. The snuba_params fixture is built but unused by any test.

Transaction test asserts count of 1 for a query that filters on transactions in an errors-focused path

test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events stores a transaction and expects count 1 in bucket one and 0 in bucket two, but the earlier error events fall in those same buckets with the errors query path; the expectation does not clearly isolate the transaction behavior and may pass for the wrong reason.

Unrelated error message change alters public API response text

The topEvents validation message is changed from 'If topEvents needs to be at least 1' to 'topEvents needs to be at least 1'. This is unrelated to upsampling and changes an API response string that clients or tests may match on.

Upsampling is applied to the wrong columns: transform occurs only when top_events or rpc, and reassigns final_columns after use

The transform is computed inside each branch using query_columns, but final_columns is initialized once and the rpc/top-events branches each recompute from query_columns, so behavior is correct only by accident. More importantly, count() is rewritten to 'upsampled_count() as count' even though the response consumers and the zerofill/other-column logic expect the count alias semantics; the alias is embedded in a column string rather than passed through the normal parser, which may break equations and orderby referencing count().

upsampled_count aggregate ignores sample_weight semantics and returns sum over all rows

The new upsampled_count function is defined as toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no check that sample_weight is non-null. Events without sample_weight (or from non-allowlisted projects in mixed queries) contribute null/zero, silently undercounting, and the transform's comment that the schema guarantees the column exists is unverified. Also default_result_type 'number' is inconsistent with the 'integer' type used by count().

Typo in comment ('segements') and loose null handling

The added comment contains a typo. More importantly, the early return for max_segment_id None is correct, but the MatchedRow type change is not reflected in fetch_rows_matching_pattern's query, which still uses max() that can return null for groups with no segments.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Used backup code is stored as null inside the JSON array and never removed, leaving null entries and a race window

After a successful backup-code login, `backupCodes[index] = null` is written back as JSON. Subsequent lookups call indexOf on the array, so the used slot is null and cannot match, which is correct, but the array is never compacted and the update is a read-modify-write with no guard. Two concurrent logins with the same valid backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either writes, so one code can be used twice. The update should be conditional (compare-and-set on the stored ciphertext) or done in a transaction.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
backupCodes state typed as never[] and the download URL is never revoked on close

useState([]) infers an untyped empty array, so backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode) and the render path rely on loose typing. Also the blob URL created in handleSetup is only revoked when a new setup starts; resetState and the close button do not revoke it, so the backup codes text remains in memory until the next setup.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code login and backup code flows are not tested end to end

The only new test covers download, copy and close on the setup screen. Nothing exercises logging in with a backup code via Lost access, a used code being rejected, or disabling 2FA with a backup code. The PR description says the change was tested manually, but the TODO left in the file confirms the login path is untested.

Backup code path skips the TOTP check and does not consume the used backup code

When a backupCode is supplied, the handler validates it against the stored list but never removes the matched code. The code comment says 'we delete all stored backup codes at the end', but the final prisma.user.update only sets backupCodes to null when the 2FA disable succeeds. The disable path therefore accepts a backup code and still succeeds, which is intended, but the matching code is not invalidated if the update fails. More importantly, the backup-code branch runs whenever req.body.backupCode is truthy, so a request that also includes a valid-looking backupCode bypasses the TOTP requirement entirely; this is the intended lost-access flow, but nothing ties it to the login flow's rate limiting, so brute force against the 10 short hex codes is unthrottled on this endpoint.

Backup codes have only 40 bits of entropy and are stored in a rate-unlimited path

Each backup code is 5 random bytes (10 hex chars, about 40 bits). Combined with the login path, which only applies the general checkRateLimitAndThrowError per email, this makes online guessing of a single code feasible for a motivated attacker over time, and it weakens the 2FA guarantee. Longer codes or a stronger rate limit on backup-code attempts would be expected.

Backup-code error codes are mapped in onSubmit but IncorrectBackupCode is not in errorMessages, and the login form reuses totpCode for the 2FA step

Errors thrown from authorize surface as res.error values. The branch-based mapping works, but the login form still submits the TOTP input value as totpCode when in backup mode, and the backupCode field is only populated when the user is in lost-access mode. If the user switches back from lost access, methods.setValue('backupCode', '') is called but the stale totpCode is not cleared in that path, so a previously typed TOTP can be sent with a backup code, causing authorize to take the backup branch and ignore the code the user intended.

JSON.parse and decrypt on user.backupCodes can throw an unhandled error for corrupt data

symmetricDecrypt and JSON.parse run without try/catch. Malformed or legacy ciphertext produces an unhandled exception that returns a 500 with no error code instead of MissingBackupCodes or IncorrectBackupCode, and the same unguarded parse exists in next-auth-options.ts authorize.

Lost-access toggle is only reset on success, so switching modes keeps stale backup code input and errors

The lost-access button calls resetForm(false) which clears backupCode and totpCode but the form is also used with a shared totpCode field. Toggling mode also does not reset the TwoFactor/BackupCode field registration, and on success the code only resets form values, not the mode, relying on setTwoFactorLostAccess(false) which is fine, but a failed attempt in backup mode leaves errorMessage from the previous mode visible until the next submit.

Setup overwrites backup codes and secret before 2FA is enabled, and never clears them on failed enable

Setup writes new backupCodes and a new twoFactorSecret while twoFactorEnabled stays false. The backup codes are shown to the user only after the TOTP enable step, but the codes stored are the ones returned by this call. If the user abandons setup, the previous state is replaced anyway; this is acceptable, but the backup codes are also accepted at login only when twoFactorEnabled is true, so the display-before-enable ordering means users see codes that are not yet active. Verify the enable endpoint persists the same codes it displayed, since nothing in the diff shows the enable handler changed.

onEnable is only called on close, so the parent refreshes state only after the user dismisses backup codes

Previously onEnable() fired right after the TOTP code was accepted. Now it fires only when the user clicks close on the backup codes screen. Closing the dialog via onOpenChange or the Dialog's X button skips onEnable and resetState, so the parent never learns 2FA was enabled and the modal's step is left on DisplayBackupCodes when reopened.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fallback sets refresh_token to the literal string 'refresh_token'

When the response has no refresh_token, the function writes the placeholder string "refresh_token" into the parsed data. That value is then persisted to the credential, overwriting the real refresh token with a garbage value, so future refreshes against the provider fail.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Minimum token schema uses computed string keys, not a real schema for expiry

The keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are computed property names evaluating to the literal string "ZodString"/"ZodOptional" etc. The schema therefore does not validate any expiry field and the 'any property with a number is the expiry' intent is not implemented. Under sync mode, refreshed tokens are accepted without checking expiry_date/expires_in, and callers that rely on expiry (e.g. Google, Zoom) can store undefined expiry, causing tokens to be treated as expired or never refreshed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Salesforce token refresh now always hits the network and ignores the stored token and the sync path

getClient unconditionally POSTs to login.salesforce.com on every service construction, with no expiry check, and no sync-endpoint branch via refreshOAuthTokens, unlike other apps. This changes behavior for every Salesforce calendar operation (extra latency and requests per call), and self-hosters using sync will still hit Salesforce directly. The response.statusText !== 'OK' check is also fragile since HTTP/2 responses may have empty statusText, causing false failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Refreshed Salesforce key drops fields and writes parsed data that excludes instance_url

The persisted key is `{...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token}` but salesforceTokenSchema parses only listed fields, and zod strips unknown keys. Salesforce's refresh response includes instance_url, and it is in the schema, so that holds, but other stored fields like the original `expiry` info are lost; additionally the connection now uses credentialKey.instance_url (old) rather than the refreshed one.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Decryption and JSON.parse errors are unhandled and produce 500s; invalid input is not validated

symmetricDecrypt and JSON.parse on reqBody.keys are not wrapped in try/catch, and appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse throws a ZodError rather than returning a 400. Malformed or wrongly encrypted payloads cause unhandled exceptions. Also an empty CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY is passed as '' rather than rejected.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync endpoint fetch has no error handling and no auth header

The fetch to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends the user id and app slug without any authentication, and the response is returned unchecked. A non-2xx response or HTML error page is returned as if it were a token response; callers like Google (`res?.data`) and Hubspot then treat it as valid tokens. Also the refresh path for user credentials is entirely bypassed when sync is on, so a failure in the sync endpoint silently breaks refresh with no fallback.

false_negatives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

false_positives.candidate:
APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string or undefined, not a boolean

The expression evaluates to the env string (or undefined), not a boolean. It is used in `if` checks and returned in the webhook gate, which works by truthiness but the exported type is misleading and an empty-string secret is treated as disabled while whitespace is enabled. Should be wrapped in Boolean().

App lookup and metadata lookup are redundant and the credential is matched on the wrong field

The code looks up the app by slug, then looks up appStoreMetadata by app.slug and uses appMetadata.slug for the credential appId. The DB app row is only used for existence. Credential matching by userId+appId via findFirst also does not restrict type, so an existing credential of a different type for the same app would be overwritten with new keys. Creation sets type from metadata but updates never reconcile type.

CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME added to globalEnv out of alphabetical order and duplicates exist

The new env vars are inserted out of order, and INTERCOM_SECRET was already duplicated in the list. Minor, but the list is clearly maintained sorted and this makes future diffs noisier.

CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME comment says lowercase but code reads it directly from req.headers

Node lowercases incoming header names, so the code works only if the env value is lowercase. The comment states the requirement but the code does not normalize it, so a mixed-case value silently fails with 403 for every request.

No tests cover the new sync path or the parse fallback behavior

The PR adds a new sync mode affecting ~15 apps, a new webhook endpoint, and parse fallback logic, but the PR checklist states no tests were added. Bugs such as the broken zod schema and the 'refresh_token' placeholder would have been caught by unit tests.

Redirect URI hardcoded to zoho-bigin, changing the slug-based value

The redirect URI was changed from using appConfig.slug to a literal string. This is harmless now but removes the single source of truth and must match callback.ts, which still uses appConfig.slug; any future slug change will break the OAuth redirect mismatch.

Removed error logging and tokenResponse.success check changes failure behavior

The zod-failure console.error was removed, and parseRefreshTokenResponse now throws on invalid responses instead of returning a failed result. The code then still spreads `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data`, which is dead logic since the function either throws or returns a successful result. Errors from Microsoft (e.g. invalid_grant) now surface as an unhelpful error instead of being logged with the MS response.

Webex expiry only updated when expires_in present, leaving stale expiry_date

The refreshed token only updates expiry_date if expires_in is present, and the refresh path is now reachable through sync which may omit expires_in. The stored expiry_date then stays in the past, causing a refresh on every call.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality and undefined-safe

The header is compared with `!==` against process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET. If the env var is unset, the header is undefined on requests without it and undefined === undefined passes, but the code path is guarded only by APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED. Also the comparison is not timing-safe. Use crypto.timingSafeEqual and explicitly reject when the secret is empty.

Zoho CRM callback expiryDate adds 3600 ms instead of seconds

Math.round(Date.now() + 60 * 60) adds only 3.6 seconds, not one hour, so the stored expiryDate is effectively now and tokens are immediately treated as expired.

Zoho CRM expiry is hardcoded to one hour regardless of response

zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.expiryDate is set to Date.now()+60*60 (missing *1000 is fine but expires_in is ignored), which is an existing pattern but now also runs for sync-supplied tokens whose lifetime may differ, so tokens can be treated as valid after expiry.

Zoom refresh computes expiry from expires_in which is absent in sync mode

After parseRefreshTokenResponse, key.expiry_date is set from newTokens.expires_in * 1000. In sync mode the minimum schema does not require expires_in, so expires_in can be undefined, producing NaN expiry_date and a token that is never considered expired or always considered expired depending on comparison.

prisma is used but never imported in CalendarService

getClient now calls prisma.credential.update, but the file imports no prisma client (the import list has no `prisma`). This is a compile/runtime ReferenceError when a Salesforce credential is used.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

getCalendarCredentials stores unawaited promises that can reject unhandled

false_positives.candidate:
Async forEach callback in requestReschedule ignores its returned promises

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` discards the promises from `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` and `deleteMeeting`. The mutation then sends the reschedule email and resolves, while calendar and video cancellations are still running. Any rejection is unhandled and invisible to the caller. Async forEach callback makes the try/catch useless and drops rejections

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` does not await the callbacks. The `try/catch` only catches synchronous throws, so failures from `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting` become unhandled rejections and are never logged. Recurring cancellation pushes to apiDeletes after it has already been awaited

Any same-day date override makes a slot available and skips all busy-time checks

When any date override exists on the slot's day and the slot is not rejected by the override range checks, `dateOverrideExist` is set and the function returns `true` before evaluating `busy`. A slot that overlaps a calendar event or existing booking for a fixed host is therefore reported as available, which is the exact double-booking the PR is meant to prevent.

The override matching logic only tests the day of `date.start` against the slot start day. true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of what its name and the design promise

`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is named to check that errors do not block offset commits, and the worker's `finally` marks a failed item as complete. So offset 101 is committed after 100 fails. The test instead asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which requires no commit. The check also runs only 0.2s after processing, before the 1s commit loop runs, so it passes by timing rather than by design. The assertion should verify that the commit reaches 102 (the next offset after 101), and the sleep should be replaced by a wait for the commit.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
A never-arriving offset stalls commits for the partition permanently

In `get_committable_offsets`, the loop breaks at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Offsets can legitimately skip on compacted or transactional topics, or when a message is dropped before submit. When that happens, the highest committable offset can never advance past the hole because the missing offset is never added. Commits for that partition then stop until restart, and the consumer group's lag grows indefinitely. The skipped offset should be treated as complete, for example by tracking the next expected offset from the broker rather than assuming contiguity.

Kafka commit function is invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own thread and calls `self.commit_function`, which calls the arroyo `commit` callable provided by the StreamProcessor. The rest of the arroyo pipeline (and the consumer) is driven from the processor thread, and the commit callable and the Kafka consumer are not documented as thread-safe. Calling commit concurrently with poll or with rebalance handling can cause races or errors during partition reassignment. Commits should be issued from the processing thread, for example in `poll`.

Kafka integration test leaks processor and topic on assertion failure and bypasses the factory it claims to test

The processor is shut down only on the success path, and the factory is shut down there too, so a failed assertion leaves the StreamProcessor and its queue threads running. The `KAFKA_TOPIC_OVERRIDES` override is also set but never used by the StreamProcessor, which takes the topic explicitly, so the override is misleading. The `finally` block only deletes the topic and swallows all exceptions. Move processor and factory cleanup into `finally`, and remove the unused override.

Queues are unbounded, so the advertised backpressure does not exist

Each per-queue `queue.Queue()` is created without a maxsize, and `submit` calls `work_queue.put` without blocking limits. The class docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing ever fills up. If a slow downstream handler or a stalled worker falls behind, in-memory work items and their Kafka message payloads accumulate without bound while the consumer keeps polling and fetching. Either bound the queues and make submit block or apply poll-side pausing, or remove the claim from the docstring.

Tests rely on fixed sleeps and polling of internal queue stats, which makes them flaky

Most new thread-queue tests poll `queue_pool.get_stats()` and `call_count` in loops with `time.sleep(0.1)`, then assert the result without any event. The commit tests can pass before the 1-second commit thread has run, and `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` only checks commits that happened to occur within the window. Use threading events or the `wait` helpers already used in queue_consumer tests so the tests are deterministic instead of depending on scheduler timing.

Names and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so (name='a_b', parent='') and (name='a', parent='b') produce the same key. A denial for one resource would then be applied to another. The key also shares the '.perm_' prefix with userPermCacheKey, so it can collide with permission-cache entries if identifiers contain '_'. A separator that cannot appear in these fields, or a hash of the tuple, is needed.

Denial cache is consulted before permissions, so a cached denial defeats the fix for newly created resources

Check now returns a cached denial (keyed by user, action, name and parent folder) before looking at permissions. The denial is written at line ~153 whenever a check is denied and lives for shortCacheTTL (30s). The PR's stated goal is that a creator can access a dashboard or folder they just created. If the creator (or anyone) is checked for that name before it exists, the denial is cached. Once the resource is created and the user gets access, the next Check still hits the denial cache and returns Allowed=false for up to 30s. The new 'requery from DB on cache miss' logic never runs in that window. Name-less checks (create verbs, where Name is empty) are cached the same way, so a denied create can block a subsequent allowed create for 30s. Denials should not be cached for resources that may be created, or the denial cache should be invalidated when permissions change.

The denial entry is set for every denied request, with no regard for whether the target exists yet or whether Name is empty. For verbs like create (Name empty), checkPermission returns len(scopeMap)>0, so a user with no permissions is denied and that denial is cached under a key with an empty name. Any later create within 30s is denied from cache even after the user is granted permissions. Caching negatives this broadly also means permission revocations are not reflected for the TTL of the denial, which is not documented.

TestService_CacheCheck covers an explicit denial entry, a cache miss, and an outdated cache, but none checks the scenario this PR targets. A user is denied for a resource, the resource is then created and the permission granted, and the next Check must allow. The 'explicit deny' test seeds the denial cache by hand and only checks that denial wins. Without a test for the denial-then-grant sequence, the bug above goes unnoticed. The new branch of the logic is therefore largely untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine progress messages logged at Error level on every batch

The new fetch-then-delete loops log informational messages with `r.log.Error(...)`: 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', 'Annotations to clean by count', 'cleaned annotations by count', 'Tags to clean', and 'cleaned tags'. These run for every batch, including batches that delete nothing, and they fire every cleanup cycle (once a minute now). This will flood error logs and trigger error alerting even on healthy systems. They should be Debug (or Info) messages. The `err` key is also always nil in the success-path log lines, which is misleading.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unrelated change: cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The diff changes `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` in `Run`. This is not mentioned in the PR description and has nothing to do with the MySQL deadlock fix. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, annotations) run ten times as often, with a 9-minute timeout per run. This should be reverted or split into its own PR with a stated rationale.

false_positives.candidate:
Fetched IDs are deleted without re-checking the condition, so the delete is not guarded

The IDs are selected in one statement and deleted in a separate one with no transaction. Between the two, a concurrent update could change a row so it no longer matches (for example, a row's `created` changes). This is probably acceptable for cleanup, and the comment acknowledges the under-delete case, but the delete statement does not repeat the age or type condition, so a row that no longer qualifies can still be removed. Consider including the original condition in the DELETE, or document this explicitly as accepted behaviour.

Full ID lists logged on every batch, potentially up to the batch size

Each batch logs the full `ids` slice (`"ids", ids`), and the batch size is configurable and can be as large as 32767 in the new test. Each cleanup batch therefore writes tens of thousands of IDs into the log, repeated on every batch and every cycle. Log the count only, or log IDs at Debug level.

Large-batch test inserts about 40k rows on every run and is gated only by -short

The new case inserts 40003 annotations and 80006 annotation_tag rows through the store in 500-row batches for each of the three cleanup cases. This is slow on every integration run and is the only coverage of the SQLite parameter limit path in `deleteByIDs`. The SQLite-specific inline-ID branch has no unit test that checks the generated SQL or the case where the batch size exceeds 999 on a non-SQLite database. Consider a unit test for `deleteByIDs` SQL generation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete attaches the parent logger instead of the scoped log

ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) in Delete discards the log with name/kind/method values that was just built, so downstream logs lose context. Inconsistent with other methods.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection async legacy duration is recorded with the storage metric

The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records its outcome with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, corrupting storage vs legacy metrics.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete storage duration metric records the object name as the kind label

In Delete, recordStorageDuration is called with `name` in the kind position instead of options.Kind, so the metric label cardinality explodes per object name and the kind dimension is wrong, unlike every other method.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy write uses the request ctx, which is cancelled when the request returns

The goroutines launched in Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection derive their context from the request ctx via context.WithTimeoutCause. When the HTTP request finishes, the request context is cancelled, so the legacy write is aborted almost immediately after the response is sent. The 'asynchronous safe measure' write will frequently fail silently (only logged/metric'd), leaving legacy out of sync. The background goroutine should use a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx)) plus the timeout.

Create passes the same obj to legacy asynchronously after storage may have mutated it

The goroutine calls d.Legacy.Create with the same obj and options that were just passed to Storage.Create, concurrently with the returned object being used by the caller. Storage Create/Update implementations can mutate the object (e.g. set ResourceVersion, UID, generated name), so the legacy write races with those mutations (data race detected by -race) and may write different content than what was stored in unified storage.

Mode 3 tests do not verify the asynchronous legacy write happens

The tests set up legacy mock expectations but never assert they were called, and the goroutine can race with test teardown. Failures in the legacy write (the core of mode 3 behavior) are untested; the Update failure test has no legacy expectation at all.

New mode 3 integration cases are not tied to legacy consistency checks

The new mode 3 cases run the same doPlaylistTests, which asserts only unified-storage results; since legacy writes are asynchronous and not awaited, the tests cannot detect the legacy write being lost, so the added coverage does not validate the feature.

Update error path records a legacy metric for a storage failure

When Storage.Update fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration, so storage failures are counted as legacy errors and storage error metrics are never incremented for update.

Update goroutine leaks the context cancel on a path that never calls cancel promptly

In Update, the context.WithTimeoutCause is created in the goroutine, but cancel is deferred after the timer is set and it is fine; however the cancel is only called after Legacy.Update returns. The ctx variable is shadowed correctly, but the timeout starts before startLegacy is measured; minor, though combined with the request ctx cancellation the goroutine has no independent lifetime control.

Update reuses objInfo for legacy after storage consumed it

objInfo is an UpdatedObjectInfo whose UpdatedObject is typically called by Storage.Update, and the same objInfo is then passed to the async legacy Update. The legacy update will run the transform again against the current stored state of legacy (or a different old object), and it may race with the storage call that is still using objInfo. The previous implementation carefully wrapped the storage result for the legacy write; that was removed, so legacy may get a different object than what was written to unified storage.

options.Kind dereferenced for nil-safe access and CreateOptions has no Kind field used reliably

log uses options.Kind on *metav1.CreateOptions etc.; these option types' Kind is set only via TypeMeta and is often empty, so the logs/metrics label is frequently blank. Mode 3 metrics labels depend on this.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No double-check after acquiring the write lock

After the RLock check at lines 41-47 fails, the goroutine takes the write lock without re-reading `entryPointAssetsCache`. Every goroutine that observed a nil cache at the same time will repeat the full manifest load and CDN fetch, and each will overwrite the global in turn. The lock prevents a data race, but it does not prevent this duplicated work or the last-writer-wins churn on a cold start.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No test covers the concurrent access this change is meant to fix

The PR fixes a data race on the package-level cache, but it adds no test that exercises `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines. Without a `-race` test, nothing guards against regressions. A test that runs concurrent calls in both dev and non-dev modes would verify the fix.

Write lock is held across CDN and file I/O, blocking all readers

The write lock is acquired at line 48 and held via defer for the whole rebuild, including `readWebAssetsFromCDN`, which performs an HTTP request bounded only by the caller's context. While a cache miss or dev-mode reload is in progress, every concurrent `GetWebAssets` call blocks on `RLock` at line 41, even though a valid cached value may exist. Before this change, readers never blocked. A slow or hung CDN can therefore stall all page renders that go through this function.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false, so the feature flag has no effect

The function computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)`, returns false if enabled, and then returns false unconditionally. The result is that SQL expressions are disabled regardless of the flag. The logic is confusing and suggests a half-finished edit. If the intent is a hard kill switch, the function should simply return false with a comment saying so, and the feature-flag lookup should be removed. As written, a maintainer reading the flag check would believe the flag gates the feature.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stub DB makes every SQL expression fail, including legitimate ones

TablesList, RunCommands and QueryFramesInto all return 'not implemented'. Because `sql.TablesList` in parser.go depends on RunCommands, `NewSQLCommand` now fails for every query. The SQL expression type is therefore completely non-functional, not just locked down. This is a deliberate hotfix, but nothing in the PR documents that the feature is gutted, and the stubbed DB type is named as if it were a real in-memory database. This should be an explicit, documented temporary state.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message says 'not implemented' for a deliberate security disable

Users who enable sqlExpressions will get 'sqlExpressions is not implemented', which misstates the situation. The message should say the feature is disabled for security reasons and point to the advisory. Operators trying to diagnose it will be misled.

No tests added for the disabled SQL path

The PR changes the reader's behaviour for QueryTypeSQL and removes a dependency, but adds no test asserting that SQL expression queries are rejected. A regression test is needed so that the gate cannot be silently removed, and a test for UnmarshalSQLCommand to confirm the bypass is closed.

Quote-escaping is still used to build SQL via fmt.Sprintf

TablesList still interpolates user SQL into a string with fmt.Sprintf after only doubling single quotes. This is the injection-prone pattern that the RCE/LFI issue is about. It is currently unreachable because RunCommands is stubbed, but it will be dangerous as soon as a real engine is reconnected. Keeping this code path unchanged in a security fix is risky.

The SQL gate is only in the reader; NewSQLCommand and UnmarshalSQLCommand have no gate

The disable check lives only in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery. `UnmarshalSQLCommand` in sql_command.go calls `NewSQLCommand` directly and never checks the gate. Any other caller that builds an SQL command bypasses the disable. It currently fails only because the stubbed `sql.TablesList` always returns an error. That is incidental, not a guard, so a future change to the DB stub would reopen the vulnerability. The check should be enforced in `NewSQLCommand` or at the execution boundary.

tablesFromAST indexes ast[0] without checking length

`flatten.Flatten(ast[0], ...)` panics if the slice is empty, for example if the JSON decodes to `[]`. The code is unreachable today, but the panic would become reachable as soon as the stub is replaced.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the whole-function lock allows duplicate index creation for the same key

The lock previously serialized BuildIndex, which also prevented two concurrent builds of the same NamespacedResource from both calling bleve.New on the same directory / overwriting each other. With the lock removed, getOrCreateIndex (GetIndex returns nil, then build) can run concurrently for the same key from Search and handleEvent, leading to two bleve indexes opened on the same file path (bleve.New fails with 'index already exists' or corrupts state) and one index silently replacing the other in the cache. The PR narrows the lock to only the map write, which does not protect this path.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding the lock

BuildIndex now writes b.cache under cacheMu, but TotalDocs (called from searchSupport.init logging) ranges over b.cache with no read lock. Concurrent builds during init (errgroup with multiple workers) can cause a concurrent map read/write, which is a fatal runtime error in Go. TotalDocs should take cacheMu.RLock().

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on totalBatchesIndexed and shared err in init goroutines

Inside group.Go closures, totalBatchesIndexed++ is written concurrently by multiple goroutines without synchronization, and the shared outer variable err is assigned from concurrent goroutines (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`). This is a data race; the err assignment can also return the wrong error. Use a local error variable and an atomic counter.

Eager Init in constructor makes startup failures fatal and can block/crash the process

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) which runs lifecycle init, the full search index build over all resources, and starts the watcher. Any error (e.g. DB not ready, index build failure) now causes the constructor to fail, and the index build runs synchronously with no timeout before the server is returned. The PR's own reviewer note asks what this could break; callers of NewResourceServer (module wiring, tests) must now tolerate long blocking startup and a hard failure. Also the ctx used is the server's internal background-derived context, so no caller cancellation applies.

History, Origin and Search dereference nil search support

After removing the Init guard, History and Origin call s.search.History / s.search.Origin directly. When search is not configured (opts.Search.Resources == nil or Backend nil, so s.search is nil), these methods panic with a nil pointer dereference. Previously the nil Init path did not guard this either, but Search has an explicit nil check while History/Origin do not.

No tests cover the new eager initialization or the lock change

The behavioral change (init moved into constructor, per-RPC Init removed, locking changed in BuildIndex) has no accompanying unit test for concurrent BuildIndex or for NewResourceServer returning an error when init fails. The module server test change only adds a skip for postgres, which does not validate any of the changes.

Stop() overwrites initErr and Init's once guard hides subsequent failures

Init uses sync.Once and stores the error in s.initErr; Stop sets s.initErr to a 'stopping' error. Since Init is no longer called on each RPC, a failed init is only reported once from the constructor, and any caller that later calls Init gets a stale or misleading error. Combined with removing the per-RPC Init checks, a server whose init partly failed (e.g. lifecycle ok, search failed) silently serves requests with no index or no watcher.

Watch context is detached from the init trace context and goroutine loops forever on channel close

The watcher goroutine loops `v := <-events` without handling a closed channel; when the poller exits (closed stream), v becomes nil and handleEvent dereferences evt.Type, panicking. Also the watch context is context.Background() so it is never cancelled on server Stop, leaking the goroutine.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers a bogus alias, so the 20 IDPs created by the test are never removed

The cleanup `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` uses the literal string "alias" instead of the created IDP's alias. Every registered cleanup therefore targets a nonexistent provider and removes nothing. The IDPs `idp-alias-0..20` (including the hidden `idp-alias-20` and the org-linked ones) leak into the shared test realm and can change results of other tests that call getForLogin or list IDPs. The same pattern exists in testCacheIDPByOrg, but the new test copies it. The fix is to capture the alias in a final variable and remove that alias.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
null and empty-string organizationId map to the same cache entry but can produce different results

`searchKey` is `organizationId != null ? organizationId : ""`, so a null organizationId and an empty-string organizationId share the same key. In the delegate, a null organizationId means 'any org' for ORG_ONLY/ALL, while "" is passed as a literal organization id to the ORGANIZATION_ID filter. For ALL mode the cached result for one can be served for the other, returning wrong IDPs. Use a distinct sentinel or key on Objects.toString with a prefix to avoid the collision.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns a random keystore provider instead of a BC provider

getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(default type).getProvider(), which is whatever provider supplies the default keystore (usually SUN/JKS), not BouncyCastle. Callers that expect BC (e.g. BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER lookups) get the wrong provider, and the method creates a keystore instance each call. Most other operations in this provider throw UnsupportedOperationException, so the BC provider mismatch is a real contract break for any code path that reaches it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead ASN1Encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 create ASN1Encoder instances and call write(...) whose results are discarded. These are no-ops that only add confusion; the actual encoding is done again at lines 117-121. Harmless functionally but indicates a copy/paste leftover that a maintainer would want removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
readSequence loop can run forever or miscount on zero-length elements

In readSequence, the loop subtracts bytes.length from the remaining length per element. readNext returns header plus content; if the decoded length is inconsistent with the sequence, length may never reach zero or may go negative without error, and a malformed element with an indefinite-length marker (-1) is not rejected. Malformed input can cause misparsing or a hang risk rather than a clean IOException.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks all existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() was added as an abstract interface method. Any third-party or out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation will fail to compile or load. A default implementation would avoid breaking the SPI contract.

false_positives.candidate:
Test only checks round trip of concatenated form, not DER correctness

The test asserts asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) == x, but never verifies that the DER output verifies against the original JDK signature or matches the JDK-produced DER. A symmetric bug in both directions would pass. It also uses the EC keypair generated with default curve without checking the curve matches the algorithm's expected size.

concatenatedRSToASN1DER produces non-minimal/signed-incorrect DER integers

r and s are built with a leading zero byte and passed to new BigInteger(r) then re-encoded via BigInteger.toByteArray(). This yields a correct minimal two's complement encoding, but the input is assumed to be unsigned big-endian of length signLength/2 with no check on signLength; if signLength is odd or the array is shorter than expected, System.arraycopy throws ArrayIndexOutOfBounds at runtime rather than a clear error. The method also never validates that signature.length >= signLength.

getKeyStore ignores the format's provider and uses KeyStore.getInstance without provider

getKeyStore returns KeyStore.getInstance(format.name()) which uses the format name directly (e.g. 'PKCS12' or 'BCFKS' names) and may fail for formats not in the default JDK, while DefaultCryptoProvider uses format.toString() and BC provider. Inconsistent behavior with the other providers.

logger.debugf used with a non-constant format string

The 'Ignored crypto providers' message is built as a string and passed as the format to debugf. Any '%' in class names would be misinterpreted as a format specifier. Use debugf with a format argument instead.

order() of 100 makes the minimal provider win over full providers only if others are absent; CryptoIntegration selects by highest order

CryptoIntegration sorts by order descending and picks the first. AuthzClientCryptoProvider has order 100 while DefaultCryptoProvider, Elytron and FIPS have 200, so they win when present. However, AuthzClientCryptoProvider is registered via META-INF/services in the authz-client jar, and AuthzClient.create() calls CryptoIntegration.init() which is a no-op if a provider was already set. In the Keycloak testsuite and any app with both on classpath, the initialization order decides the provider, making behavior depend on who initializes first. The selection is therefore not deterministic for this design.

readInteger uses signed BigInteger from DER without validation

readInteger reads raw bytes and calls new BigInteger(bytes) which is correct for DER two's complement, but it does not reject empty content (length 0), which throws NumberFormatException instead of IOException, and readLength returning -1 (indefinite length) is passed directly to read(-1) causing NegativeArraySizeException. Malformed signatures from a server can therefore surface as unchecked exceptions.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NPE when the all-clients resource is missing

In the fallback branch, getResourceTypeResource(...) can return null (for example when the schema is not supported or the Clients resource has not been created). The next line then calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) with a null resource, which causes an NPE on every client permission check instead of returning false. A null check is needed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Client removal now calls setPermissionsEnabled, which throws in V2

The ClientRemovedEvent branch calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). With ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose clients() now returns ClientPermissionsV2. That class's setPermissionsEnabled (ClientPermissionsV2.java around line 193) throws UnsupportedOperationException. Deleting any client in a realm with V2 enabled will therefore fail or leave the realm in an inconsistent state. The listener should skip the V2 path, or ClientPermissionsV2 should implement the call as a no-op or resource cleanup.

Per-client resource shadows the all-clients grant

hasPermission(client, scope) only evaluates the client's own resource when one exists (lines 214-222). The all-clients fallback runs only when no resource exists for that client. If an admin has a realm-wide 'all clients' VIEW permission and later creates a client-specific permission for another scope on the same client, a resource is created for that client. The all-clients VIEW grant is then no longer considered for that client, and the admin loses access they should still have. The fallback should be evaluated in addition to, not instead of, the per-client resource.

requireView() javadoc describes a boolean return instead of a throw

The javadoc for requireView() says 'Returns true if canView() returns true', but the method is void and should throw ForbiddenException when canView() returns false. The same wrong wording appears for requireViewClientScopes(), and the requireList/requireListClientScopes docs are similarly inconsistent with their methods.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
Existing RECREATE exit code silently changed from 4 to 3

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE moves from 4 to 3, and the new FEATURE_DISABLED takes 4. The command's exit code is a documented contract for CI/CD scripts (the update-compatibility guide tells users to branch on it). Any pipeline that treats 4 as 'rolling upgrade not possible' will now misread a feature-disabled condition as a recreate requirement, and the old value now means something else. The change is only justified if the old code 4 was never released; the PR does not state this, and the new code should be checked against the released behaviour.

Feature gate runs before config validation and depends on Profile being initialised

Profile.isFeatureEnabled dereferences Profile.getInstance() and unboxes features.get(feature). If Profile has not been configured, or the feature key is absent from the map, this throws a NullPointerException instead of a clean CLI error. Nothing in the PR guarantees Profile is initialised before run() is reached.

Feature setup overwrites any existing enabled features

setEnabledFeatures(List.of(ROLLING_UPDATES)) replaces the whole enabled list rather than appending to it. If getTestKeycloakDeployment or a future caller sets other enabled features, they are silently dropped. Merge the lists instead.

Null-strategy deployments never enable rolling-updates, but the operator now requires it

createInitialDeployment returns early when updateStrategy is null, before the FeatureSpec with rolling-updates is set. The PR's own docs say the operator fails when rolling-updates is not enabled. The null-strategy case of testCacheMaxCount expects eventuallyRollingUpgradeStatus, so that test will run against an operator with the feature disabled and fail or behave incorrectly. The feature enablement must happen for every case, not only after the early return.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission adds resource name where group IDs are expected by callers

In V2 the resource for a group is looked up by ID (hasPermission(groupId,...) calls resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)), so resources are named by group id; this is consistent. However the V2 loop over findByType adds groupResource.getId() (the internal resource UUID) to the granted set, not the group ID/name. Callers (UsersResource, BruteForceUsersResource, getUsersCount) pass this set to session.users() as group IDs, so the filter compares the wrong identifiers and group-based user visibility silently returns nothing for V2.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

false_positives.candidate:
Group listing no longer lets users with view-only global access see all groups

The previous code computed canView() once and short-circuited the per-group check. The new code calls groupsEvaluator::canView per element, which for V2 performs a permission evaluation per group (performance regression) and, combined with the now-empty set semantics, can filter out groups a caller with global view should see if canView(group) does not short-circuit on global roles consistently.

Permission resource ID check drops scope grants from all-users permissions

hasPermission now requires permission.getResourceId().equals(resource.getId()). When evaluated against the all-users resource type resource, permissions returned are associated with that resource, but for user-specific resources the matching resource may be a different one; additionally getResourceId may be null for some permission types, causing NPE. The added check changes semantics without test coverage.
