This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer interpolated into JavaScript without escaping

`'<%= request.referer %>'` is placed inside a script literal. ERB HTML-escapes but a referer containing a single quote or backslash-sequence is not JS-escaped, so the value can break out of the string literal in the inline script.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same XSS risk: request.referer is interpolated into an inline JavaScript string without JavaScript escaping, allowing malicious referer content to break out of the literal.

false_positives.candidate:
Raw HTML from remote feeds/pages stored and rendered without sanitization

Posts created by import use cook_method raw_html, so `Post#cook` returns the raw content unchanged. Content comes from remote RSS feeds or fetched third-party pages (import_remote uses Readability output, but PollFeed passes `i.content` directly). Script or event-handler markup from an untrusted source is rendered to all viewers of the topic and in the embed iframe, a stored XSS vector.

open() of user-configured URL with Kernel#open allows command injection on old Rubies and no timeout

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses Kernel#open, which on Ruby versions before 3.0 treats strings starting with '|' as shell commands. The URL is an admin setting, but it also has no timeout, so a hung feed server blocks the scheduled job indefinitely. Use URI.open or a Net::HTTP call with timeouts.

Kernel#open on a fetched URL in import_remote

`open(url).read` is used on an URL that comes from embed requests (TopicRetriever passes the embed_url from an unauthenticated controller parameter, validated only by host). Kernel#open with a crafted string and no timeout can hang or execute commands on old Rubies, and the fetch has no size or time limit.

Anonymous requests can enqueue unbounded retrieve jobs

For any unknown embed_url, `best` enqueues a :retrieve_topic job for every request. The throttle is applied only inside the job (retrieved_recently? via redis), so a flood of distinct URLs on the embeddable host queues an unbounded number of jobs, each performing an outbound HTTP fetch.

Port handling drops explicit default ports inconsistently and prefix may be built on nil host

`uri.host` is nil for URLs without a host, and the `prefix << ':port'` line mutates a string that may be frozen in some configurations. Also non-default ports on https (443 check only applies to one scheme) produce wrong absolute URLs for http on 443 or https on 80.

contents mutated in place with <<

`contents << ...` mutates the caller's string. In PollFeed, `content` is built once per item and reused; in TopicRetriever/import_remote the doc.content string is mutated, and the sha1 comparison on re-import now includes the footer added each time, so the footer is appended on every import call to the same string object.

Throttle key set with setnx then expire is non-atomic

setnx followed by a separate expire can leave the key without a TTL if the process dies between calls, permanently throttling that URL. Use SET with NX and EX in one command.

user.try(:staff?) passes nil when no user, but args may be a Sidekiq hash with string keys

Jobs are serialized through Sidekiq, so args keys become strings after serialization in some paths; `args[:user_id]` and `args[:embed_url]` may be nil, causing the InvalidParameters raise or silently skipping the user lookup.

Disqus import no longer applies category option and removes the option entirely

The --category option was deleted and the category handling removed, but the import now calls TopicEmbed.import_remote which fetches each thread's live URL instead of creating topics from the XML data. Imports now depend on network access to the old site and ignore the Disqus message content, a behavior change not reflected in the description or help text.

raw_html posts skip the cooking pipeline and plugin filters entirely

cook returns raw when cook_method is raw_html, bypassing Plugin::Filter :after_post_cook and all sanitization. Any post set to this method, including ones edited later, is stored unsanitized, and the before_save hook also calls cook so edits reuse raw content. Combined with the import path this is a security regression across the whole post model.

Adding NOT NULL column with default rewrites entire posts table

add_column with default and null: false on a large posts table locks and rewrites every row in PostgreSQL on older versions, blocking writes during deploy on large forums.

Unique index on embed_url with no length guard for string column

embed_url is a varchar with no length limit, and a unique btree index on long URLs can exceed PostgreSQL's index row size limit, causing inserts of long embed URLs to fail with an error that is not handled in TopicEmbed.import.

force: true on create_table will drop existing top_topics data

Adding force: true means that rerunning or running this migration on an installation where the table exists silently drops and recreates it, deleting all TopTopic rows without any warning.

save with skip_validations silently ignores failures

`@post.save(validate: ...)` return value is ignored, so a failed save (for example a validation error when skip_validations is false) leaves the in-memory post changed and save_reply_relationships still runs, and the caller receives true from revise!. Errors go unreported.

embeddable_host and feed settings exposed without validation

embeddable_host is an unvalidated string used as the sole referer check and also to decide which hosts to fetch from. No default validation or type constraint exists, so an admin mistake (e.g. a bare wildcard or empty string on a site that does not set it) can open the embed endpoint to any host.

Success assertions run in an after hook and do not verify the behaviour under test

The `after` block asserts response success and headers, but after blocks in the success context also run for the test that expects TopicRetriever and for the TopicView test where render behaviour differs. Failures are reported confusingly and the tests do not check that the loading template is rendered on the retrieve path.

No test for security-relevant behavior: HTML injection through URL and raw content

The spec asserts raw_html rendering but never tests that the embed URL is escaped in the footer or that script content is neutralized. The security regressions introduced by raw_html storage are unchecked.

PollFeed item processing and error paths are untested

Only the guard conditions and delegation are tested. poll_feed (parsing items, falling back to i.id, CGI unescaping, import) has no coverage, and the spec requires an unrelated process_post job file.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side size limit now hardcoded to 10MB, removing the per-type site setting

The `max_' + type + '_size_kb` site setting lookup was replaced with a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated downsize passes a percentage to gifsicle --resize-fit

The controller calls `downsize(..., "80%", allow_animation: ...)`. For GIFs, `optimize` routes to `downsize_instructions_animated`, which calls `resize_instructions_animated` and emits `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. gifsicle's `--resize-fit` expects a WxH geometry, not a percentage, so the resize fails. `convert_with` returns false, the controller ignores that, and animated GIFs over the limit are never reduced. Animated GIFs need a separate code path or an explicit scale that gifsicle accepts.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: animated GIF downsizing passes a percentage (80%) to gifsicle --resize-fit, which expects WxH geometry, so resizing fails and oversized animated GIFs are not reduced.

true_positives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Downsize loop ignores failure and retries the same conversion up to 5 times

`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns false when conversion fails (`convert_with` swallows errors), but the loop doesn't check the return value. A failed conversion leaves the file unchanged, so the loop runs all five attempts on identical input, wasting time, and then proceeds to `Upload.create_for` with an oversized file. The loop should stop on failure, and the oversized case should be reported to the user rather than silently accepted. Also, `tempfile.size` may be stale if the tool replaces the file rather than rewriting it in place, so the loop condition needs verification.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same stale tempfile.size concern affecting the downsize loop condition, despite also discussing conversion failure handling.

false_positives.candidate:
Client rejects files over 10MB before the server can downsize them

The feature is meant to accept large images and shrink them server-side, but this client check rejects any file larger than 10MB before upload. Users uploading large images will still see the error, so the feature is ineffective from the UI. The check needs to allow images above the limit (or skip it for images) to match the server behavior.

HTTP 413 message now hardcodes 10MB instead of the configured image limit

The 413 branch previously showed `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. It now always displays 10 MB, so the error text can disagree with the actual configured limit that the server enforces.

API URL download limit changed from the site setting to a hardcoded 10MB

The remote URL download cap was switched from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a fixed `10.megabytes`. This changes the API contract: admins who lowered the image size setting no longer constrain downloads, and the 10MB cap is not configurable.

No tests for the new large-image downsize path

The change adds automatic downsizing in the upload controller, changes the `OptimizedImage` method signatures, and changes client validation, but the PR includes no specs. Nothing covers the loop, its failure handling, animated GIFs, or the duplicate `downsize` definition.

PR description is not meaningful

The description is only 'Test 1'. It does not explain the behavior change, the removal of the site-setting-based limits, or the 10MB hardcoding, so reviewers cannot assess the intent.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.

Two concurrent logins with the same valid backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either writes, so one code can be used twice. The update should be conditional (compare-and-set on the stored ciphertext) or done in a transaction.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same race condition: concurrent backup-code logins can both pass the in-memory check before either write completes, allowing one code to be accepted twice. The candidate adds a secondary note about null entries, but the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code path skips the TOTP check and does not consume the used backup code

When a backupCode is supplied, the handler validates it against the stored list but never removes the matched code. The code comment says 'we delete all stored backup codes at the end', but the final prisma.user.update only sets backupCodes to null when the 2FA disable succeeds. The disable path therefore accepts a backup code and still succeeds, which is intended, but the matching code is not invalidated if the update fails. More importantly, the backup-code branch runs whenever req.body.backupCode is truthy, so a request that also includes a valid-looking backupCode bypasses the TOTP requirement entirely; this is the intended lost-access flow, but nothing ties it to the login flow's rate limiting, so brute force against the 10 short hex codes is unthrottled on this endpoint.

Backup codes have only 40 bits of entropy and are stored in a rate-unlimited path

Each backup code is 5 random bytes (10 hex chars, about 40 bits). Combined with the login path, which only applies the general checkRateLimitAndThrowError per email, this makes online guessing of a single code feasible for a motivated attacker over time, and it weakens the 2FA guarantee. Longer codes or a stronger rate limit on backup-code attempts would be expected.

Setup overwrites backup codes and secret before 2FA is enabled, and never clears them on failed enable

Setup writes new backupCodes and a new twoFactorSecret while twoFactorEnabled stays false. The backup codes are shown to the user only after the TOTP enable step, but the codes stored are the ones returned by this call. If the user abandons setup, the previous state is replaced anyway; this is acceptable, but the backup codes are also accepted at login only when twoFactorEnabled is true, so the display-before-enable ordering means users see codes that are not yet active. Verify the enable endpoint persists the same codes it displayed, since nothing in the diff shows the enable handler changed.

onEnable is only called on close, so the parent refreshes state only after the user dismisses backup codes

Previously onEnable() fired right after the TOTP code was accepted. Now it fires only when the user clicks close on the backup codes screen. Closing the dialog via onOpenChange or the Dialog's X button skips onEnable and resetState, so the parent never learns 2FA was enabled and the modal's step is left on DisplayBackupCodes when reopened.

Lost-access toggle is only reset on success, so switching modes keeps stale backup code input and errors

The lost-access button calls resetForm(false) which clears backupCode and totpCode but the form is also used with a shared totpCode field. Toggling mode also does not reset the TwoFactor/BackupCode field registration, and on success the code only resets form values, not the mode, relying on setTwoFactorLostAccess(false) which is fine, but a failed attempt in backup mode leaves errorMessage from the previous mode visible until the next submit.

Backup-code error codes are mapped in onSubmit but IncorrectBackupCode is not in errorMessages, and the login form reuses totpCode for the 2FA step

Errors thrown from authorize surface as res.error values. The branch-based mapping works, but the login form still submits the TOTP input value as totpCode when in backup mode, and the backupCode field is only populated when the user is in lost-access mode. If the user switches back from lost access, methods.setValue('backupCode', '') is called but the stale totpCode is not cleared in that path, so a previously typed TOTP can be sent with a backup code, causing authorize to take the backup branch and ignore the code the user intended.

JSON.parse and decrypt on user.backupCodes can throw an unhandled error for corrupt data

symmetricDecrypt and JSON.parse run without try/catch. Malformed or legacy ciphertext produces an unhandled exception that returns a 500 with no error code instead of MissingBackupCodes or IncorrectBackupCode, and the same unguarded parse exists in next-auth-options.ts authorize.

Backup code login and backup code flows are not tested end to end

The only new test covers download, copy and close on the setup screen. Nothing exercises logging in with a backup code via Lost access, a used code being rejected, or disabling 2FA with a backup code. The PR description says the change was tested manually, but the TODO left in the file confirms the login path is untested.

This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

The function also returns `true` and sends the reschedule email before the cancellations have run. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: async callbacks inside forEach are not awaited, so try/catch cannot handle rejections and cleanup/error handling is incomplete. The candidate's suggested fix (for...of with await or Promise.allSettled) aligns with the golden recommendation.

false_positives.candidate:
Import promises are created eagerly, so every app module loads at import time

Each entry is written as `import("./x")`, which starts loading the module as soon as the object literal is evaluated. Any module that imports appStore therefore loads all ~28 app modules up front, which defeats the purpose of async loading. Wrapping each entry in an arrow, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, would defer loading until a caller asks for the app. Callers would then need to invoke the function instead of awaiting the property. Also, a rejected import that nobody awaits becomes an unhandled rejection.

Async forEach callback makes the try/catch useless and drops rejections

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` does not await the callbacks. The `try/catch` only catches synchronous throws, so failures from `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting` become unhandled rejections and are never logged. The function also proceeds to send the email before the cancellations finish. Use `for...of` with `await`, or `Promise.allSettled`.

Recurring cancellation pushes to apiDeletes after it has already been awaited

The `forEach(async (credential) => ...)` callback awaits `getCalendar` and then pushes `deleteEvent` promises into `apiDeletes`. Nothing waits for these callbacks, and `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` runs later with the array as it was at that point. Calendar deletions for recurring bookings may therefore be skipped from the awaited set, and their rejections go unhandled. Replace this with a `for...of` loop that awaits each credential.

Async forEach callback in requestReschedule ignores its returned promises

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` discards the promises from `getCalendar`, `deleteEvent` and `deleteMeeting`. The mutation then sends the reschedule email and resolves, while calendar and video cancellations are still running. Any rejection is unhandled and invisible to the caller. Use `for...of` with `await` or `Promise.allSettled`.

Video adapters are resolved one at a time instead of in parallel

The `for...of` loop in `getVideoAdapters` awaits each `appStore` import in sequence. The dynamic imports are independent, so this serializes module loading for every video credential. `Promise.all` over the credentials would avoid the extra latency.
